thread.title: What is Prop 2? Exploring the citizen-led proposal to limit corporate campaign spending
thread.title_full: What is Prop 2? Exploring the citizen-led proposal to limit corporate campaign spending

author: Rebecca Borlace
title: What is Prop 2? Exploring the citizen-led proposal to limit corporate campaign spending
text:
Michigan voters will decide Nov. 3 whether to approve Proposal 2 — also known as the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics Initiative — a citizen-led proposal seeking to limit corporate influence in politics.
If passed, the proposal would ban utility companies, contractors who receive more than $250,000 annually from the government and organizations or individuals with “substantial connections to those utilities and contractors” from making contributions to campaigns that could benefit them. The ban would apply to races for governor, attorney general, secretary of state, the state legislature and certain local offices, as well as ballot measure committees.
The proposal would also expand transparency regulations on political communication spending by requiring disclosure of donor information for online ads — even those that do not expressly tell voters who to vote for.
Michiganders for Money Out of Politics initiated the proposal. Since their formation in July 2025, the group has gathered more than 560,000 signatures in support of Prop 2.
According to a WDIV/Detroit News poll conducted in early September, the proposal is overwhelmingly popular, with 71.5% of Michigan voters planning to vote yes.
Business sophomore Aarzu Patni, an early voter, told The Daily she voted yes on Prop 2 because it will increase transparency around campaign finance.
“I was thinking that funding for political parties shouldn’t come from things like that that might have hidden motives,” Patni said. “That’s why I put yes for it. … In general, as much control as there is around funding that political parties receive, the better, because you know (it) can kind of influence their decisions a lot.”
In an interview with The Daily, LSA senior Aaron J. Puno, who is currently running for Ann Arbor School Board , said he supports Prop 2 because he believes elections should be based on ideas rather than funding and connections.
“I will be enthusiastically voting yes on November 3, and I don’t know a single person in my life who plans to vote and isn’t going to vote for this thing,” Puno said. “These elections ought to be campaigns of ideas, as opposed to campaigns of how big your ad budget is and what favors you can call in.”
Puno criticized companies like DTE Energy , saying they are more focused on generating shareholder value than on investing in better infrastructure for Michiganders. Similar companies that would be impacted by the campaign restrictions include Consumers Energy and Xcel Energy .
“Instead of investing these profits into shoring up their infrastructure to provide a more reliable product for the people of Michigan, which would in turn increase their profits, they’ve chosen to prioritize short-term — short-term interests, short-term profits by buying back stocks,” Puno said.
In an interview with The Michigan Daily, public policy professor Devin Judge-Lord, who studies federal campaign contributions, said he expects Prop 2 to pass in Michigan based on similar campaign finance restriction ballots in states like Maine.
Judge-Lord said he thinks Prop 2 will reduce the power of large government contractors on policy. He added that, by narrowing political spending options, companies may have less of an opportunity to take advantage of loopholes and price gouge.
“I think the main objective here is to attempt to reduce the power that they have over policy,” Judge-Lord said. “That then affects our electricity rates, the quality of the grid and how often our electricity goes out — or the quality of the healthcare that we receive and the cost of our premiums, etc.”
Primary backlash for Prop 2 comes from Protect MI Free Speech , a campaign formed specifically to oppose the measure. In a statement to CBS News Detroit , John Sellek, a spokesperson for Protect MI Free Speech , said the proposal could infringe on freedom of speech as it restricts individuals with “substantial connections” from donating to relevant campaigns.
“Voters should oppose Proposal 2 because it uses voter frustration with the cost of living as cover to carry out a much wider sneak attack on the freedom of speech rights of thousands of innocent, everyday Michigan residents who would be banned from supporting the candidates of their choice simply because of who they are related to or contract with,” Sellek said. “Meanwhile, out-of-state billionaires can continue spending as they please to influence Michigan’s public policy making.”
Prop 2 has received criticism , with Michael Van Beek of the Mackinac Center for Public Policy calling its terms “vague” and “undefined,” and its ban on contributions from individuals with “substantial connections utilities and contractors” overly-restrictive.
Judge-Lord said the debate around the “substantial connections” language hinges on how many people it would restrict if passed, which remains undetermined. He said courts will likely decide the clause’s scope.
“‘Substantial connections’ will probably be interpreted by the people implementing the law and the judges reviewing the law as ‘substantial connections’ for the purpose of reducing the power of large government contractors and monopoly utilities in government policymaking,” Judge-Lord said.
Prop 2 will be on the ballot this midterm election. Early voting is happening between Oct. 21 and Nov. 1.
